messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] waic
parts:
Hi, this question is tougher than it looks!  We were actually going to have a section in the waic paper regarding the comparison of models but we removed it because it was getting so difficult to interpret.  The traditional view is that the difference is compared to a chi-squared distribution with df corresponding to the difference in number of parameters but that doesn’t work in general.  Beyond this, it’s fine to pick a model that doesn’t fit if it is more useful in some other way.  Consider all the work on variable selection and dimension reduction, where it is considered a benefit to have a model with fewer parameters.
A

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] waic
parts:
Hi, in that case I prefer model A.  The only issue is what is the prior for the slope.  Given that model B is in the picture, I’m guessing you don’t want a flat prior for the slope in model A.  From this perspective, model B is a special case of a N(0,0) prior on the slope, and it’s hard to imagine that this is a good idea, at least not in the sorts of problems that I work on.
A

As WAIC is on the same scale as AIC(c) and DIC, I believe that Anderson & Burnham's rules of thumb still apply. If I recall correctly, a difference of <= 2 from the minimum implies strong support, between 4 and 7 implies some support, > 10 implies no support for model.

Avi

I'm paraphrasing greatly, as my Burnham and Anderson text isn't at home. The rule of thumb is simply given two models, if the difference between the XIC values is <= 2, the second model isn't really "worse" or won't perform worse than the one with the min XIC. IF the difference is > 10, it is very likely that it will perform worse. Forgive my abuse of terminology.

Avi

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: waic
parts:
You can use the same approach for WAIC as for cross-validation. See section 2.3 in Aki Vehtari and Jouko Lampinen (2002). Bayesian model assessment and comparison using cross-validation predictive densities. Neural Computation, 14(10):2439-2468. http://becs.aalto.fi/en/research/bayes/publications/VehtariLampinen_NC2002_preprint.pdf  This works very well when p_eff << n/2.  If p_eff is relatively high compared to n, the approach provides a useful indicator, but it's not so well calibrated (we are investigating this).

I have also used thumb rules similar to what, e.g,  Burnham and Anderson mention. Often they work, but sometimes there is much more variation in WAIC (or CV) estimates and these thumb rules can then be misleading. Usually this happens if there are a small number of observations with a very low predictive density, ie. they are far in the tails of the predictive distribution and even small changes in the model can change the predictive density a lot for these.

Aki
